object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Represents the customer in the system.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six-digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered, identified by product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets: seats, API access, SSO -- the feature bundle shown on the pricing page.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Name of a feature bundle, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Unique.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription starts; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual. ... Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled. ... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag on a subscription indicating it is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with an effective date and requester; represents the history behind the subscription's current plan.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date ... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan normalised to a month, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used for three distinct concepts: the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and the sales-negotiated deal mentioned by Tom. The sales-negotiated 'plan' is not modeled here since it was explicitly deferred to another meeting. Clarify whether this third concept needs to be captured in this model or remains out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan

ambiguities.description: The external uniqueness 'one active subscription per account per product' only applies to subscriptions with active-like status, not to all subscriptions historically. The model does not have a clean way to scope the uniqueness constraint to only 'active' status subscriptions (it may need to include cancelled/past subscriptions with different products/accounts). Clarify exactly which statuses count toward this uniqueness rule.

source_references.excerpt: One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag is described as a separate boolean that overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (a paused subscription might still show as 'active' status). It's unclear whether Paused should be modeled as an additional constraint (e.g., exclusion with certain statuses) or left as an independent, unconstrained attribute as stakeholders describe it as a known source of bugs. Clarify the intended relationship between PausedFlag and SubscriptionStatus.

source_references.excerpt: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The business rule for what happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term (run to term, prorated refund, or credit) is explicitly undecided/parked. Only the system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured. Clarify whether a refund/credit concept should eventually be modeled once finance and legal decide the policy.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Manual credits/refunds given as goodwill (mentioned as happening four times last quarter) are referenced but not modeled as a fact type since they exist 'outside the subscription' system and their structure isn't described. Clarify if these need their own entity/fact type for completeness.

source_references.excerpt: the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether the relationship between Account and its history is meant to be tracked at all -- when an account closes and the company returns, a new account number is issued and treated as a new customer, losing history. Clarify whether any cross-account linkage (e.g., 'same company, different account') should be modeled, since Tom raised this as a product concern.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad ... because it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The FeatureBundle identifier is 'name' with no code, which Tom finds problematic ('There's no code, which annoys me'). While confirmed unique, this is a fragile identifier prone to future issues (e.g., renaming). Clarify if a more stable code-based identifier is planned.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Is the name unique? ... Yes.

ambiguities.description: The 'current price plan' on Subscription is described as denormalised/derived from the PlanChange history, yet also asserted as a real stored field. It's ambiguous whether this should be modeled as a stored fact type (as done here) or purely as a derived/computed value like MRR, especially since Priya states 'if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug' -- implying the change history is authoritative and current plan could be seen as derived, similar to MRR.

source_references.excerpt: there's a denormalised current plan on the record ... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.
